'''''Chloris gayana''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the common name '''Rhodes grass'''. It is native to Africa but it can be found throughout the tropical and subtropical world as a [[introduced species|naturalized species]].

It can grow in many types of habitat. It is also cultivated in some areas as a palatable [[grazing|graze]] for animals and a groundcover to reduce [[erosion]] and quickly revegetate denuded soil.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.tropicalforages.info/key/Forages/Media/Html/Chloris_gayana.htm |title=Tropical Forages |access-date=2009-03-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171017033750/http://www.tropicalforages.info/key/Forages/Media/Html/Chloris_gayana.htm |archive-date=2017-10-17 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is tolerant of moderately [[soil salinity|saline]] and [[alkali soil|alkaline soils]] and irrigation.<ref>[http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Chloris_gayana.html Purdue Horticulture]</ref>{{rp|2}}

==Description==
This is a perennial grass which can reach one half to nearly three meters in height and spreads via [[stolon]]s. It forms tufts and can spread into wide monotypic stands. The [[inflorescence]] is a single or double whorl of fingerlike racemes up to 15 centimeters long. Each spikelet in the raceme is a few millimeters long and contains one or two fertile florets and up to four sterile florets.

==Growing conditions== 
Its seasonal growth is in the spring and summer and its rainfall requirement is 600–750 mm per year.<ref name="fao.org">[http://www.fao.org/ag/agp/AGPC/doc/Gbase/data/pf000199.htm] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170619035356/http://www.fao.org/ag/agp/AGPC/doc/Gbase/data/pf000199.htm |date=2017-06-19 }} Chloris gayana, Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations</ref> This low rainfall requirement means that this grass can survive in drier places. Rhodes grass can grow in a variety of soil conditions.<ref name = "Suttie">{{cite book |last1=Suttie |first1=J. M. |author2=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations |chapter=Hay Crops – Cereals and Grasses |pages=63–86 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZYcDhblVEssC&pg=PA63 |title=Hay and Straw Conservation: For Small-scale Farming and Pastoral Conditions |date=2000 |publisher=Food & Agriculture Org |isbn=978-92-5-104458-2 }}</ref> Its ideal soil would be anything greater than a 4.3 pH level in terms of acidity.<ref name = "Sanford">{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=Geoff |last2=Sanford |first2=Paul |last3=Wiley |first3=Tim |title=Perennial pastures for Western Australia |journal=Bulletins |publisher=Department of Agriculture and Food, Western Australia |date=1 December 2006 |url=https://researchlibrary.agric.wa.gov.au/bulletins/1/ }}</ref>{{rp|2}} In addition to this, ''Chloris gayana'' has a moderate aluminum tolerance.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|2}} The fact that this type of grass survives on little rainfall, can grow in low pH soils, and has a moderate tolerance to aluminum means that it may be beneficial to poor farmers in the sub-tropics. Less work is required to maintain this grass which means that the farmers can focus on other priorities. It is also beneficial to farmers who own land with poor soil.

Benefits from ''Chloris gayana'' can also be found in the plant's growth. The seed germinates quickly (1–7 days) depending on temperature.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|2}} and it often achieves full ground cover within three months of sowing.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|2}} This too is good for farmers when it comes to covering bare soil. The fact that ''Chloris gayana'' can grow quickly means that farmers could use it to protect the soil from eroding.

==Stress tolerance== 
An important feature of ''Chloris gayana'' is its drought tolerance.<ref name = "Ponsens">{{cite journal |last1=Ponsens |first1=J. |last2=Hanson |first2=J. |last3=Schellberg |first3=J. |last4=Moeseler |first4=B.M. |title=Characterization of phenotypic diversity, yield and response to drought stress in a collection of Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana Kunth) accessions |journal=Field Crops Research |date=July 2010 |volume=118 |issue=1 |pages=57–72 |doi=10.1016/j.fcr.2010.04.008 }}</ref>{{rp|70}} The reason why it is drought tolerant can be found in its roots. Production may effect with mild drought period if it is cultivated for forage purpose. ''Chloris gayana'' roots are able to extract water at a depth of 4.25 meters.<ref name="fao.org"/> Since this grass has good drought tolerance, it could also be beneficial to farmers for ensuring livestock are fed in times of drought.

Another important feature of ''Chloris gayana'' can be found in its salt tolerance. In terms of grass species, this type appears to be one of "the most salt-tolerant species"<ref name = "Deifel">{{cite journal |last1=Deifel |first1=Kurt S. |last2=Kopittke |first2=Peter M. |last3=Menzies |first3=Neal W. |title=Growth Response of Various Perennial Grasses to Increasing Salinity |journal=Journal of Plant Nutrition |date=September 2006 |volume=29 |issue=9 |pages=1573–1584 |doi=10.1080/01904160600848870 |s2cid=85308838 }}</ref>{{rp|1583}} in terms of grasses. In "saline conditions, plant growth is restricted".<ref name="Deifel"/>{{rp|1574}} Since ''Chloris gayana'' shows good salt tolerance, this type of grass can be beneficial to farmers who have salinity problems in their soil.

==Genetic stocks==
There are various genetic varieties of ''Chloris gayana'' that exist like Katambora, Pioneer and Callide. "Katambora" is an important genetic variety that originates from Zimbabwe.<ref name="fao.org"/> It has been found to be more persistent on poorer soil than other genetic varieties.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|1}}<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|3}} Katambora is meant for hay production because it is leafier, finer-stemmed, and produces better dry matter.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|3}} "Katambora" is diploid type.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|3}} Diploid types of ''Chloris gayana'' in general show good frost tolerance, salt tolerance, and drought tolerance.<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|3}}

A different type of ''Chloris gayana'' are tetraploid types. Tetraploid types of ''Chloris gayana'' have a major characteristic in which they flower late in the season which means the feed quality is maintained longer<ref name = "Sanford"/>{{rp|3}} It has also been determined that tetraploid varieties of ''Chloris gayana'' have "higher concentrations of nutrients".<ref name = "jones">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=R. J. |last2=Loch |first2=D. S. |last3=LeFeuvre |first3=R. P. |title=Differences in mineral concentration among diploid and tetraploid cultivars of rhodesgrass (Chloris gayana) |journal=Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture |date=1995 |volume=35 |issue=8 |pages=1123–1129 |id={{ProQuest|48310796}} |doi=10.1071/ea9951123 }}</ref>{{rp|1128}} Both tetraploid and diploid varieties at the pre-flowering stage of growth have "adequate concentrations of nutrients".<ref name="jones"/>{{rp|1128}} Understanding the different genetic varieties of ''Chloris gayana'' is beneficial to farmers. Knowing the different types will allow a farmer to choose what is best for their situation.

==Practical information== 
''Chloris gayana'' can be very helpful to farmers and NGOs in terms of sustainable agricultural development. Pasture establishment for farmers "demand high capital cost and labour."<ref name = Tadesse>Tadesse, Alemu (1990), The Unexploited Potential of Improved Forages in the Mid-Altitude and Lowland Areas of Ethiopia, Institute of Agricultural Research Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, http://www.fao.org/wairdocs/ilri/x5536e/x5536e10.htm#establishment_of_improved_forages_in_natural_pastures</ref> A possible solution to this would be to intercrop ''Chloris gayana'' with food crops. This would be economically feasible for resource poor farmers.<ref name="Tadesse"/> ''Chloris gayana'' can be undersown to maize after final weeding of the crop without affecting maize grain yield.<ref name="Tadesse"/> In addition to this, "growing cultivated forages, in association with food crops, can contribute to the improvement of the qualitative and quantitative supply of livestock feed."<ref name = "Hassen">{{cite journal |last1=Hassen |first1=A. |last2=Gizachew |first2=L. |last3=Rethman |first3=N. F. G. |last4=Niekerk |first4=WA van |title=Influence of undersowing perennial forages in maize on grain, fodder yield and soil properties in the sub-humid region of western Ethiopia |journal=African Journal of Range & Forage Science |date=1 March 2007 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=35–41 |doi=10.2989/102201107780178168 |hdl=2263/5772 |s2cid=54080270 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>{{rp|38}} Intercropping ''Chloris gayana'' with a food crop is a practical method farmers can use when it comes to sustainable agricultural development.

There are some practical tips that farmers should be aware of when it comes to harvesting ''Chloris gayana''. For example, "the crop is most productive in the first two or three cuts".<ref name="Suttie"/> The [[nutritional value|nutritive value]] of this forage is high when the grass is young, but it decreases with maturity.<ref>Heuzé V., Tran G., Boudon A., Lebas F., 2016. Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/480 Last updated on April 15, 2016, 14:23</ref> Farmers should be aware of this in order to make sure that they can take full advantage of this type of grass. In terms of grazing, ''Chloris gayana'' should be grazed when the weather is not appropriate for harvesting.<ref name="Suttie"/> This too is important for being able to use this type of grass efficiently.

There are other practical uses that farmers can benefit from when growing ''Chloris gayana''. It can help with weed control because it can outcompete and smother weeds.<ref name = "Smith">{{cite report |last1=Valenzuela |first1=Hector |last2=Smith |first2=Jody |title=Rhodesgrass |date=August 2002 |hdl=10125/12746 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>{{rp|2}} In addition to this, ''Chloris gayana'' is also able to deal with soil erosion on sloped fields by holding [[topsoil]].<ref name="Smith"/>{{rp|2}} ''Chloris gayana'' can also be mixed with legumes such as cowpea, stylo, and alfalfa which also improves soil nutrient levels.<ref name="Smith"/>{{rp|3}} Managing weeds, soil erosion, and improving the soil are all important issues a farmer must deal with. ''Chloris gayana'' can be a good option for a farmer when it comes to trying to solve these problems.
